An implementation-approximated facility is one that defers its definition to an external source while recommending an ideal behaviour. While conforming implementations are free to choose any behaviour within the constraints put forth by this specification, they are encouraged to strive to approximate the ideal. Some mathematical operations, such as Math.exp, are implementation-approximated.

outcomes.note: Spec requires bit-exact IEEE binary64 for + - * / and correctly-rounded sqrt (sqrt is defined as the square root of the real value, rounded to a Number), so these agree across engines. Math.sin/cos/exp/pow-class functions are 'implementation-approximated': engines may differ in last bits. A shared n-body step using them cannot be assumed bit-identical across browsers; chaotic/sensitive dynamics then amplify the difference (about 6e4x over 1e5 steps here). Mitigation space: avoid transcendental calls in the sim loop (use only + - * / sqrt, own sin/cos polynomials), fixed step, server-authoritative state with periodic resync. Math.pow/atan2 text not separately quoted; they sit in the same approximated family per spec text for sin (not verified verbatim here). Cross-browser run not performed.

outcomes.note: Float addition is not associative; reordering three gravity terms changed ship position by 9.65e-10 after 1e5 steps on one machine. Hamilton's equations of E_mu are equivalent to q'' = -mu (q-m(t))/|q-m(t)|^3 - (1-mu)(q-e(t))/|q-e(t)|^3

the discrete mapping obtained describes the exact time evolution of a slightly perturbed Hamiltonian system and thus possesses the perturbed Hamiltonian as a conserved quantity. This guarantees that there is no secular change in the error of the total energy
If the integrator is not symplectic, the error of the total energy grows secularly in general.
ship position difference vs 1e-12 perturbation: 5.9e-8 at 1e5 steps

outcomes.note: Kepler two-body motion is analytic: position at any time t comes from a closed-form solve of Kepler's equation, so any client can evaluate state at any t without stepping (random access, no drift, cheap, identical inputs give the same output up to the solver's tolerance). In the restricted problem the primaries can still be put on analytic Kepler orbits (the quoted model prescribes m(t), e(t)), but the ship's trajectory has no closed form and must be stepped; error then accumulates (phase error grows, symplectic bound applies to energy only, and only for constant step as Yoshida states; the Lee-Duncan-Levison abstract notes that naively varying the step destroys the property). Race consequences: ship state is a function of the whole input history, so all clients need fixed dt and identical inputs/ordering or an authoritative server; track checkpoints/ranking cannot be computed in closed form for the ship; if bodies are N>2 mutually interacting, even the bodies are not analytic. Body count, dt and error budget are still unspecified in the brief (C-194); here dt=0.001 with 3 sources gave 1e-12 -> 6e-8 in 1e5 steps.

Not run. Experiment: for each track, (1) define the course as ordered checkpoints and a thrust cap; (2) run a bot/solver (e.g. random-shooting or CMA-ES over a thrust schedule, or a greedy-plus-search controller) with the shared fixed-step sim for many seeded trials; record completion rate and best time; a track is winnable if completion rate > 0 under the cap with a margin, and ranked fairly if two runs' progress metric is monotone along the reference solution. (3) Define progress as accumulated checkpoint index plus distance-to-next-checkpoint rather than orbital angle, and test that it never decreases for a known-good lap and handles retrograde/angle wrap (compare against angle-based progress on recorded runs). Also check no checkpoint requires a dv above the cap. Report completion rate, time spread, and rank inversions.
outcomes.would_settle: Automated solver run per track under thrust limits plus rank-inversion count between candidate progress metrics.
